Co-Chairs: Jesús Sigala-Rodríguez (email: jjsigala@gmail.com) and Stephen Spear (email: sspear@thewilds.org)
Red List Authority Coordinator: Johannes Penner (email: johannes.penner@web.de)

actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species is found at low and moderate elevations of the Atlantic versant, from northern Chiapas, Mexico, to western Venezuela (only one doubtful record from 1950) , and on the Pacific versant from central Costa Rica to northern Peru. In Central America, the elevational range of this species extends from near sea level to about 1,500 m, whereas in the Department of Cauca, Colombia, it can be found up to 2,650 m (Campbell and Lamar 2004, Castro-Herrera and Vargas-Salinas 2008, Wilson and Johnson 2010; G. Rivas pers. comm., 2013).
documentation.population: This species is uncommon in Mexico and Guatemala but locally abundant in several other parts of the range. It is relatively common in the Atlantic lowlands and humid highlands of northern Nicaragua (Sunyer et al. 2014).
documentation.habitats: This arboreal species inhabits tropical moist and wet forests, wet subtropical forest, cloud forest (only in the southern portion of the range), and montane wet forest. The record from Venezuela comes from a semiarid region (G. Rivas pers. comm. 2013). Habitats include primary and secondary forests, and coffee and banana plantations.
documentation.threats: In large portions of the range, especially in Guatemala and Mexico, threats include habitat loss and degradation resulting from deforestation and conversion for cattle grazing and banana plantations. The species is, however, capable of persisting in some modified habitats.
documentation.measures: This species occurs in numerous protected areas. Conservation needs include better information on the species' population trend.
documentation.use_trade: This species is used for venom research.
documentation.rationale: Although this species is declining in some parts of its range, it is listed as Least Concern because it is still widespread and has a substantial population size (Campbell and Lamar 2004).
